_comment: SKILL BLUEPRINT — output of the Spec agent, input to the Generator agent.
_comment2: One blueprint per standard. This is the contract the generator builds against.
subject: math
cluster: Create equations that describe numbers or relationships
description: Students translate the restrictions in a real-world modeling situation into equations, inequalities, or systems of equations and/or inequalities. They define variables, write each constraint (budget caps, resource limits, minimum requirements, non-negativity), assemble systems when several constraints act at once, and then test candidate solutions against every constraint to judge whether an option is viable (satisfies all constraints in context) or non-viable (violates a constraint or breaks a real-world rule such as a negative or non-integer count). The emphasis is on building the constraint model and interpreting solutions back in context, not on fully solving the system.
subSkills: Define variables with explicit units and meaning before writing any constraint
Translate a single verbal restriction into an equation or the correct inequality direction ($\le$, $\ge$, $<$, $>$)
Recognize and add implicit constraints (non-negativity $x\ge 0$, integer/whole-number requirements) from context
Assemble multiple simultaneous restrictions into a system of equations and/or inequalities
Test a candidate ordered pair against every constraint to classify it as viable or non-viable
Interpret a solution in context, rejecting mathematically valid answers that are non-viable in the real world (negative, fractional where whole units are required, out of domain)

problemArchetypes.name: Single budget or resource constraint
problemArchetypes.example: Notebooks cost $\$3$ each and pens cost $\$2$ each. You have at most $\$30$ to spend. Let $x$ be the number of notebooks and $y$ the number of pens. Write an inequality that represents the spending constraint. Answer: $3x + 2y \le 30$.

problemArchetypes.name: Minimum-requirement inequality
problemArchetypes.example: A booth must sell at least $50$ tickets. Adult tickets are $a$ and child tickets are $c$. Write an inequality for the requirement that total tickets meet the minimum. Answer: $a + c \ge 50$.

problemArchetypes.name: System of constraints from a scenario
problemArchetypes.example: A farmer plants $x$ acres of corn and $y$ acres of wheat on a $40$-acre field, with at most $\$2400$ for seed at $\$50$ per acre of corn and $\$80$ per acre of wheat. Write the full system, including non-negativity. Answer: $x + y \le 40,\ 50x + 80y \le 2400,\ x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0$.

problemArchetypes.name: Viability test of a candidate solution
problemArchetypes.example: For the system $3x + 2y \le 30,\ x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0$ with $x,y$ whole numbers, decide whether $(x,y) = (8,4)$ is viable. Answer: $3(8) + 2(4) = 32 > 30$, so it is non-viable; it violates the budget constraint.

problemArchetypes.name: Interpret a solution as viable or non-viable in context
problemArchetypes.example: Solving a model gives $x = -2$ buses, $y = 5$ buses. Explain whether this is viable. Answer: non-viable, because the number of buses cannot be negative ($x \ge 0$ is required), so this option must be rejected even though it satisfies the algebra.

Easy.description: Write or check a single constraint with the variables and cost/amount per unit handed directly to the student. One equation or one inequality. The main decision is the correct inequality direction. Worksheet items 1 to 5; this is the start of tier1.
constraints: Exactly one constraint to produce or verify ($ax + by \le c$ or $ax + by \ge c$ or $ax + by = c$)
Variables and per-unit values are stated explicitly; no implicit non-negativity required
Small whole-number coefficients (single or low double digits)
Viability checks, when present, plug one given ordered pair into one constraint

Medium.description: Build a small system (two constraints) or add the implicit non-negativity constraint, and test a candidate ordered pair against all stated constraints. Student must choose inequality directions and may need to define a variable. Worksheet items 6 to 10; this is the overlap zone where tier1 ends and tier2 begins.
constraints: Two simultaneous constraints, or one constraint plus required non-negativity $x\ge 0,\ y\ge 0$
Student defines at least one variable or extracts a per-unit value from the wording
Viability tests check a point against every constraint and state which one is violated
Coefficients may be larger but remain integers

Hard.description: Assemble a full system of three or more constraints (budget plus capacity plus non-negativity, or two limits plus a minimum), then interpret a given solution as viable or non-viable using a real-world rule beyond the listed inequalities (integer-only counts, a value outside the feasible context). Multi-sentence scenario; student supplies the complete model and the justification. Worksheet items 11 to 15; this is the end of tier2.
constraints: Three or more constraints including non-negativity and at least one mixed direction ($\le$ with $\ge$)
At least one implicit constraint (non-negativity or whole-number/integer requirement) must be supplied by the student
Interpretation requires rejecting a mathematically valid solution because it is non-viable in context (negative, fractional units, exceeds an unstated practical limit)
Multi-step reading: variables, per-unit values, and limits are spread across the scenario

difficultyRubric.tierSplit: tier1 = Easy to Medium (items ramp from single-constraint writing up to two-constraint systems and basic viability checks). tier2 = Medium to Hard (items ramp from two-constraint systems with non-negativity up to full multi-constraint models with context-based viability interpretation). No item overlap between tiers. The default single ramped worksheet covers Easy at items 1 to 5, Medium at 6 to 10, Hard at 11 to 15.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student reverses the inequality direction, reading 'at most' as $\ge$ or 'at least' as $\le$
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For a $\$30$ spending cap writes $3x + 2y \ge 30$ instead of $3x + 2y \le 30$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student uses an equation where an inequality is required, treating a cap or minimum as an exact amount
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Writes $3x + 2y = 30$ for 'no more than $\$30$' instead of $3x + 2y \le 30$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student omits the implicit non-negativity (or integer) constraint
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Gives only $x + y \le 40$ and $50x + 80y \le 2400$, leaving out $x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student attaches each coefficient to the wrong variable when translating
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Writes $2x + 3y \le 30$ when notebooks ($x$) cost $\$3$ and pens ($y$) cost $\$2$, giving $3x + 2y \le 30$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student accepts a mathematically valid solution that is non-viable in context (negative or fractional count)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Calls $(x,y) = (-2,5)$ viable because it satisfies the inequalities, ignoring that $x \ge 0$ is required

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student tests a candidate point against only one constraint and declares it viable
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Says $(8,4)$ is viable because $x \ge 0$ and $y \ge 0$ hold, without checking $3x + 2y \le 30$ where $3(8)+2(4)=32>30$

_comment_itemCounts: Default counts. worksheet.single = one ramped sheet (Easy->Hard across 15 items). tier1/tier2 are the two sheets if the standard is built as a complex pair (15 each; tier1 Easy->Medium, tier2 Medium->Hard, no overlap).
